reported: MAC comparison uses != instead of hmac.compare_digest(), making the token verification vulnerable to timing attacks that could allow an attacker to forge a valid signature byte-by-byte.

_verify computes the HMAC of session_id without first checking that rpartition actually found a "." separator; for a malformed token without a dot, the entire token string is treated as the session_id and HMAC-verified — this isn't exploitable by itself but wastes work on garbage input and conflates malformed tokens with valid-format ones. (Minor; the comparison will simply fail.)

hash_password uses a single round of SHA-256, which is a fast hash unsuitable for password storage — it enables efficient brute-force/g GPU cracking; a slow KDF such as PBKDF2, scrypt, bcrypt, or Argon2 should be used instead.

Sessions are only expired lazily on access, so unused expired sessions accumulate in self.sessions forever, causing unbounded memory growth (resource leak); there's no periodic cleanup or cap on session count, and an attacker calling create repeatedly can grow memory without bound.

reported: Logic bug in reserve: The method modifies stock incrementally during the check loop. If reservation fails for a later item, earlier items have already been deducted from self.stock, violating the "all or nothing" guarantee stated in the docstring.

Logic bug in release: The method sets self.stock[item.sku] to item.qty (absolute assignment) instead of adding item.qty back to the existing stock (+=). This overwrites the current stock level with the order quantity, causing incorrect inventory counts.

Potential bug in total: Division by integer literal 100 works but mixing Decimal with int in division can sometimes lead to unexpected precision contexts depending on the active Decimal context; however, strictly speaking, Decimal / int is supported. A more robust approach is Decimal("100"). I will not flag this as a definitive bug as it functions correctly in standard contexts, but it's worth noting. Correction: Actually, Decimal division by an integer is fine and preserves precision based on the context. I will remove this as a defect.

Logic bug in cancel_order: The method calls inventory.release(order) which has the bug described above (overwriting stock). Additionally, if order.status is not "placed" (e.g., "rejected" or already "cancelled"), it skips release but still sets status to "cancelled". If an order was "rejected", setting it to "cancelled" might be semantically confusing, but not necessarily a crash. However, if an order is already "cancelled", calling this again would call release? No, because status == "placed" check prevents it. But if release is buggy, cancelling a placed order corrupts inventory.

The reserve method deducts stock immediately inside the validation loop. If a subsequent item fails the availability check, the function returns False but the stock for previous items has already been decremented, leaving the inventory in an inconsistent state (violating the "nothing at all" promise).

The release method incorrectly assigns item.qty to self.stock[item.sku] instead of adding it back (+= item.qty). This overwrites the current stock level with the ordered quantity, resulting in incorrect inventory data after cancellation.

reported: bool(value) always evaluates to True for any non-empty string (including "0", "false", "no"), so setting an environment variable like APP_DEBUG=false will incorrectly set the config value to True.

config = DEFAULTS makes config a reference to the global DEFAULTS dictionary instead of a copy, causing config.update() on line 31 and assignments on line 35 to mutate the global DEFAULTS dictionary. Subsequent calls to load_config will start with the polluted defaults.

os.replace(tmp, path) is passed a string (path), but tmp was created from Path(path).with_suffix(".tmp") which only alters the suffix of the final path component. If path is a relative filename, tmp ends up in the current working directory while path is resolved relative to it, causing os.replace to fail with a FileNotFoundError due to mismatched directories.

claims.quote: The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for --disable-gil builds.
claims.claim: The free-threaded build incurs additional execution overhead compared to standard builds.

claims.quote: One thread | 6% | 5%
claims.claim: Single-threaded code runs approximately 5-6% slower on x86_64 architectures (Intel Skylake and AMD Zen 3 respectively).

claims.quote: Multiple threads | 8% | 7%
claims.claim: Multi-threaded code runs approximately 7-8% slower on x86_64 architectures, with the higher overhead partly due to bytecode specialization limits in threaded contexts.

claims.quote: However, with the GIL disabled, programs that use multiple threads should also be able to more effectively use multiple CPU cores.
claims.claim: Despite the execution overhead, free-threaded builds should achieve better overall throughput by utilizing multiple CPU cores in parallel.

claims.quote: Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non --disable-gil) builds of CPython.
claims.claim: Standard GIL-enabled builds are not impacted by these changes; the overhead is isolated to the free-threaded configuration.

claims.quote: the performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)
claims.claim: Current overhead is approximately 10% on Linux/Windows and 3% on macOS.

claims.quote: We propose a target of 20% (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance) for phase II.
claims.claim: An increase in memory usage of up to 20% is considered acceptable for the free-threaded build to be officially supported.

claims.quote: Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost.
claims.claim: Elevated memory usage is an inherent trade-off of the free-threaded design and is not expected to reach parity with standard builds without sacrificing speed.

claims.quote: It’s not a simple drop-in solution – some code will have to be redesigned to make the most of the new capability, as well as avoid performance pitfalls – but it can achieve higher performance, significantly lower latency and new thread-based functionality when embraced.
claims.claim: Free-threading requires code redesign to avoid performance pitfalls, but offers higher throughput and lower latency when properly utilized.

claims.quote: On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems.
claims.claim: Official documentation reports single-threaded performance overhead between 1% (macOS ARM) and 8% (Linux x86_64).

claims.quote: The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build.
claims.claim: Users should expect increased memory consumption when switching to the free-threaded build.

claims.quote: Free-threaded execution allows for full utilization of the available processing power by running threads in parallel on available CPU cores.
claims.claim: The free-threaded build enables true parallel execution of Python threads across multiple CPU cores.

claims.quote: That's it. I've had it. I'm putting my foot down on this craziness.
claims.claim: Curl founder Daniel Stenberg reached a breaking point regarding AI-generated bug reports in May 2025 and decided to take action.

claims.quote: We now ban every reporter instantly who submits reports we deem AI slop," Stenberg added. "A threshold has been reached. We are effectively being DDoSed. If we could, we would charge them for this waste of our time.
claims.claim: Stenberg characterized the influx of AI slop as a DDoS attack on the project and implemented an immediate ban policy for such reporters.

claims.quote: Security reports that waste maintainers' time result in confusion, stress, frustration, and to top it off, a sense of isolation due to the secretive nature of security reports," Larson wrote. "All of these feelings can add to burnout of likely highly trusted contributors to open source projects. In many ways, these low-quality reports should be treated as if they are malicious.
claims.claim: Python's Seth Larson argues that AI-generated security reports cause maintainer burnout and should be treated as malicious even if unintentional.

claims.quote: The curl security team consists of seven team members. I encourage the others to also chime in to back me up (so that we act right in each case). Every report thus engages 3-4 persons. Perhaps for 30 minutes, sometimes up to an hour or three. Each.
claims.claim: Stenberg detailed the human resource cost of AI slop, noting each report consumes significant time from multiple security team members.

claims.quote: We need to reduce the amount of sand in the machine. We must do something to drastically reduce the temptation for users to submit low quality reports. Be it with AI or without AI.
claims.claim: The curl project recognized an urgent need to reduce low-quality AI-generated reports to protect the security team.

claims.quote: because that’s what AI does. is not only the volume goes up, the quality goes down. So we spend more time than ever to get less out of it than ever. And we’re all, well, I just said, I do this full time, but the rest of the team, they’re not doing this full time. So we’re just putting a lot of burden on people and it’s actually quite sort of tiring and annoying to have to plow through this.
claims.claim: Stenberg explained that AI-generated reports are longer and more complex than previous reports, requiring more time while yielding less value, creating a burden on part-time volunteers.

claims.quote: It is a little bit of abuse because most of these, that we call them AI slop, they’re just generated by someone really quickly. They don’t really understand it, they haven’t really verified it. The AI told them this is a problem, they pass it on to us. No effort, quick, easy for them and they just hand it over to us and we get a couple of hours of work per every such instance. It doesn’t work.
claims.claim: Stenberg described the asymmetric burden where reporters submit unverified AI content with no effort while maintainers must invest hours to debunk each report.

claims.quote: We heard about this other project sort of I talked to the FFMPEG people and when they sure they get a lot of valid reports from one of these tech giants and just overload them with a lot of that’s also work.
claims.claim: Stenberg indicated that FFmpeg maintainers also face overwhelming volumes of AI-related security reports from tech companies.

claims.quote: We are just a small single open source project with a small number of active maintainers," Daniel Stenberg, the founder and lead developer of the open source app cURL, said Thursday. "It is not in our power to change how all these people and their slop machines work. We need to make moves to ensure our survival and intact mental health.
claims.claim: By January 2026, the burden of AI slop forced curl to scrap its bug bounty program entirely to protect maintainer mental health.

claims.quote: We will ban you and ridicule you in public if you waste our time on crap reports.

reported: Bug: The exponential backoff calculates delay as self.base_delay  (2  attempt), but attempt starts at 0 in the for loop. This means the first retry (attempt 0) gets a base delay of 0.5  1 = 0.5, and the first request (no retry) would have had a delay of 0.5  0.5 = 0.25 if it were retried. Standard exponential backoff typically uses 2  (attempt - 1) or starts the loop at attempt = 1 so the first delay is the base_delay itself, doubling on subsequent attempts. While not a crash, this produces a mathematically incorrect backoff sequence.

Bug: The Retry-After header value is parsed using float(retry_after). However, the HTTP specification for Retry-After allows the value to be either a delay in seconds (an integer) or an HTTP-date timestamp (e.g., "Fri, 31 Dec 1999 23:59:59 GMT"). Passing a date string to float() will raise a ValueError, which is silently caught by the except ValueError: pass block. Instead of parsing the date and waiting appropriately, the code discards it and falls back to the exponential delay, ignoring the server's explicit instruction on when to retry.

Bug: The __exit__ method returns True. In Python, returning a truthy value from __exit__ suppresses any exception that occurred inside the with block. For a context manager managing an HTTP client, there is no reason to swallow all exceptions. This will silently hide unexpected errors (like attribute errors, type errors, or logic bugs) that occur within the with block, making debugging extremely difficult. It should return False (or implicitly None).

Bug: If all attempts fail due to httpx.TransportError (e.g., connection refused), last_exc is assigned and the exception is raised correctly. However, if the requests succeed at the network level but all return retryable status codes (e.g., 503), the loop finishes and raises a RuntimeError using from last_exc. In this path, last_exc is still its initial None, resulting in RuntimeError(...) from None. This strips the useful context that the failure was due to a retryable HTTP status code, making the traceback less helpful.

reported: The loop condition while d < end: excludes the end date, contradicting the docstring which states "from start to end, inclusive". This causes the generator to miss the final date in the range.

Integer division d.month // 3 + 1 incorrectly assigns March, June, September, and December to the wrong quarter. For example, March (month 3) yields Q2 instead of Q1, and December (month 12) yields Q5 (invalid). The correct formula is (d.month - 1) // 3 + 1.

The expression d.month - 1 + months can yield a negative value when subtracting more months than the current month (e.g., adding -13 months to January). In Python, -1 // 12 is -1 and -1 % 12 is 11, so this accidentally yields the correct date, but only by relying on implementation-specific floor division behavior that differs from most languages. If months is negative enough to make month_index < -12, the year calculation becomes incorrect for dates early in the year.

reported: bool(value) always evaluates to True for any non-empty string, so setting an environment variable like APP_DEBUG=false or APP_DEBUG=0 incorrectly results in True. It should check against truthy/falsy string representations (e.g., value.lower() in ('1', 'true', 'yes')).

Assigning to config = DEFAULTS doesn't create a copy; it creates a reference to the global DEFAULTS dictionary. This causes config.update() on line 31 and config[key] = ... on line 35 to permanently mutate the module-level DEFAULTS dictionary, corrupting the defaults for all subsequent calls to load_config.

os.replace(tmp, path) passes a pathlib.Path object as the source and a str as the destination. While this works on Python 3.6+ for os.replace, the intention is clearly to use the same tmp path object that was written to. If path was config.json, tmp is config.tmp, but os.replace will atomically replace config.json (good). However, if the code was meant to just replace the extension (e.g. write to config.tmp and replace config.tmp), it fails because path doesn't have the .tmp suffix. Assuming the intent is an atomic write (write to .tmp, replace the original), it should be os.replace(tmp, Path(path)) for strict type consistency, but more importantly, it's missing tmp.chmod() to preserve file permissions, and if the original file doesn't exist, this creates a file with the default umask permissions instead of copying the existing file's permissions. Given the strict atomic-write pattern used, the lack of permission preservation is a real defect.

Assuming the intent of line 51 is an atomic safe-write, os.replace(tmp, path) correctly replaces the original file. However, there is no fsync call (e.g., f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())) before the replace. If the application crashes or loses power, the file may be truncated or partially written, defeating the purpose of the atomic os.replace pattern.

reported: The daterange function claims to be inclusive of the end date, but the while d < end condition causes it to stop before yielding end. This makes business_days (line 14) return an incorrect count (off by one) when the end date is a weekday.

The add_months function fails for negative months values. Because integer floor division (//) rounds towards negative infinity, adding a negative number of months to an early month (e.g., January) produces an incorrect year calculation (e.g., d.month - 1 + months evaluates to -1, and -1 // 12 is -1 instead of the expected 0), resulting in a wrong date or a ValueError.

The quarter function incorrectly calculates the quarter for January, February, and March. Because integer division truncates towards zero, 1 // 3, 2 // 3, and 3 // 3 all evaluate to 0, making the first three months return quarter 1 instead of 1, 1, and 2 respectively.

reported: The get method does not update the recency of the accessed key. It checks for the key and returns its value but fails to call self.data.move_to_end(key), breaking the core LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction policy. Recently accessed items will not be promoted and could be evicted prematurely.
The hit_rate method raises a ZeroDivisionError if called when the cache has recorded zero total accesses (self.hits + self.misses == 0).

The cached decorator incorrectly checks for a cache miss by testing if result is None. If the function fn legitimately returns None for some arguments, it will be treated as a miss and the function will be re-executed on every subsequent call with those arguments, defeating the purpose of the cache. It should check against a unique sentinel object instead.

reported: __exit__ returns True, which suppresses any exception raised inside the with block; a with RetryClient(...) block will silently swallow errors (including RuntimeError from get(), HTTP errors, or user bugs) and appear to succeed. It should return False/None.

Retryable-status responses (429/500/...) are discarded without being closed; if the response was streamed or the connection wasn't fully drained the connection leaks, and more importantly the final response is dropped so the caller never sees it (see next line).

When attempts are exhausted after retryable status codes (no exception), last_exc is None and the final httpx.Response (status code, body, headers) is discarded, so the raised RuntimeError reports "giving up" with no indication of the last status/response. Minor, but it hides the actual failure cause.

Sleeps (up to max_delay, i.e. 30s) even after the final attempt; the loop should break/skip the sleep when no attempts remain, wasting significant time before the exception is raised. Same for line 35.

Retry-After is capped at max_delay (30s) and only the delta-seconds form is honored; the HTTP-date form of Retry-After (allowed by RFC 9110) silently falls through to exponential backoff. Also, a literal "nan" header parses via float() and yields a 0-second delay. These are arguably intentional simplifications — I'm not certain they count as defects for your purposes.

get_json calls resp.json() without checking the status code; a non-retryable error response (e.g., 404 HTML page) raises a confusing JSON-decode error instead of an HTTP error. Also, a 2xx response with an empty body raises json.JSONDecodeError rather than anything actionable.

reported: The reserve method partially updates the stock before failing, causing an inconsistent state. If an order has multiple items and the first item has enough stock but the second doesn't, the method returns False but has already deducted the first item's quantity from self.stock, losing inventory.

The release method sets the stock to the order's item quantity (self.stock[item.sku] = item.qty) instead of adding the quantity back to the existing stock. This overwrites the current stock level, causing an inventory leak for any items that had other reservations or remaining stock.

cancel_order releases the inventory before changing the order status, creating a race condition. If another thread calls place_order on the same order concurrently before order.status is updated to "cancelled", the inventory could be reserved a second time for the same order. The order status should be updated to a "cancelling" state or this method needs a lock.

reported: The docstring says "Yield every date from start to end, inclusive," but the condition while d < end makes the range exclusive of the end date. It should be while d <= end.

Because business_days relies on the exclusive daterange, it returns the number of business days in [start, end), contradicting its own "inclusive" docstring. This results in an off-by-one error if the end date is a business day.
The formula d.month // 3 + 1 returns the wrong quarter for months 3, 6, 9, and 12 (e.g., March returns 2 instead of 1). It should be (d.month - 1) // 3 + 1.

If _days_in_month is called with an invalid month (like 13), the code attempts to create date(year, month + 1, 1) (i.e., month 14), which raises a ValueError. While internal, making the helper robust to only accept 1-12 or handling month=12 in the subtraction logic would prevent crashes.

config = DEFAULTS makes config a reference to the global DEFAULTS dictionary instead of a copy, causing DEFAULTS to be permanently mutated across multiple calls to load_config.

config.update(json.load(f)) will raise a KeyError if the JSON file contains keys that are not in DEFAULTS, because the subsequent validate(config) call on line 36 computes set(config) - set(DEFAULTS) using the mutated global DEFAULTS which now has the unknown keys removed from the difference. config.update(json.load(f)) will raise a KeyError if the JSON file contains keys that are not in DEFAULTS, because the subsequent validate(config) call on line 36 computes set(config) - set(DEFAULTS) using the mutated global DEFAULTS which now has the unknown keys removed from the difference. (Even independent of the line 26 bug, if line 26 were a copy, json.load(f) could introduce unknown keys that would rightly fail validation, but given line 26, it destructively alters the application's base defaults).

os.replace(tmp, path) passes a Path object for the source and a str for the destination. While this works on most OS, it can cause issues on some platforms (like Windows) if the file types aren't recognized identically; passing a str for both (or Path for both) is safer.

If token.rpartition(".") returns ('', '', token) when no "." is found, and token is empty, session_id will be an empty string, leading to an empty input for HMAC, which will return an incorrect mac, but if token is malformed, it can also lead to unexpected behavior. Add check for empty string or handle error.

Sessions dictionary is not thread-safe, and the get_user method can lead to a race condition. If two threads access get_user concurrently for the same expired session, one might delete the session while the other is checking its existence, leading to unexpected behavior or crashes. Consider using thread-safe data structures or locks.

Insecure password hashing using a single iteration of SHA-256, which is vulnerable to brute-force attacks. Consider using a password hashing algorithm like Argon2, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count.

claims.quote: For thread-safety reasons, an application running with multiple threads will only specialize a given bytecode once; this is why the overhead for programs that use multiple threads is larger compared to programs that only use one thread.
claims.claim: PEP 703 explains that multi-threaded programs have larger execution overhead than single-threaded ones due to bytecode specialization restrictions.

claims.quote: The largest contribution to execution overhead is biased reference counting followed by per-object locking.
claims.claim: PEP 703 identifies biased reference counting and per-object locking as the primary factors contributing to the execution overhead.

claims.quote: Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non --disable-gil) builds of CPython.

claims.quote: At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%.
claims.claim: The Steering Council's acceptance of PEP 703 outlines an expected worst-case performance penalty of 10% to 15% for the free-threaded build.

claims.quote: The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code.
claims.claim: The Steering Council mandates that any performance impact must be confined to the free-threaded build, ensuring existing GIL builds suffer no regressions.

claims.quote: The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%).
claims.claim: PEP 779 reports that current single-threaded performance penalties hover around 10% on Linux/Windows and 3% on macOS.

claims.quote: Free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance).
claims.claim: PEP 779 reports the memory use overhead of the free-threaded build to be approximately 15-20% higher than the with-GIL build.

claims.quote: We propose a target of 20% (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance) for phase II.
claims.claim: PEP 779 proposes a hard target of a maximum 20% memory use overhead for the officially supported "Phase II" stage of free-threading.

claims.quote: we propose 15% as a hard performance target.
claims.claim: PEP 779 proposes a hard performance target allowing for a maximum 15% slowdown for the officially supported "Phase II" stage of free-threading.

claims.quote: Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost.
claims.claim: PEP 779 acknowledges that higher memory usage is an unavoidable cost for safe and efficient free-threading, and that minimizing it would significantly hurt CPU performance.

reported: bool(value) does not parse string boolean representations. Since any non-empty string (including "false", "0", or "no") evaluates to True in Python, setting APP_DEBUG=false will incorrectly result in debug being True. It should parse common truthy strings or check value.lower() not in ('false', '0', 'no', 'off').

config = DEFAULTS assigns the module-level dictionary by reference instead of creating a copy (e.g., config = DEFAULTS.copy()). This mutates the global DEFAULTS dictionary when the JSON file or environment variables are loaded, causing cross-test contamination and incorrect default fallbacks in subsequent calls.

The file is opened with p.open(), but the encoding is not specified. Because it relies on the system's default encoding (e.g., locale.getpreferredencoding()), it may raise a UnicodeDecodeError on systems that default to ASCII when reading a JSON file containing UTF-8 characters. It should be p.open(encoding="utf-8").

validate(config) is called before load_config returns, but if it raises a ValueError due to a bad port or workers count, the caller cannot easily distinguish between a malformed JSON file and an invalid environment variable override. It lacks context about which source caused the validation failure.

The validation for workers is < 1, but it does not enforce an upper bound. If an environment variable like APP_WORKERS=999999999 is provided, it could lead to excessive process spawning and system resource exhaustion (fork bombing) depending on how the workers are utilized downstream.

The temporary file is opened without an explicit encoding (e.g., tmp.open("w", encoding="utf-8")). On systems where the default encoding is not UTF-8 (like some Windows or minimal Docker environments), json.dump will escape high unicode characters instead of writing them natively to UTF-8, potentially causing decoding issues later.
If json.dump raises an exception (e.g., TypeError for non-serializable values), the temporary file is created and left behind on disk because it is never cleaned up in an except or finally block.

reported: Logic error: release sets stock to item.qty instead of adding it back (+= item.qty), causing inventory counts to become incorrect (drifting towards zero or negative depending on usage).

State consistency bug: reserve mutates self.stock inside the loop; if a later item fails the availability check, the previously reserved items are not rolled back, leaving inventory in a partially reserved state.

Potential crash: quantize(Decimal("0.01")) will raise decimal.InvalidOperation if the result has more than 2 decimal places and the context rounding is not set to handle it (default rounding is ROUND_HALF_EVEN, but if the number is infinite or NaN, or if the precision is too low for the intermediate calculation, it can fail; more specifically, if discount_pct leads to a result that cannot be exactly represented with 2 decimal places without rounding, quantize works, BUT if the intermediate subtotal() - discount results in a number with excessive precision or specific edge cases, it might behave unexpectedly. However, the bigger issue is that Decimal division by 100 can produce repeating decimals if not handled, but 100 is 2^25^2 so it terminates. The real risk is if subtotal is very large or discount_pct creates a long decimal. Actually, Decimal division by 100 is safe. The real issue is that quantize requires the result to fit in the current context precision. If the default precision (28) is exceeded, it crashes. This is unlikely for normal orders but possible. A more immediate bug is that discount_pct is divided by 100. If discount_pct is "33.33", 33.33 / 100 is 0.3333. subtotal  0.3333 might have >2 decimal places. quantize handles rounding. So this is likely safe from crashes, but may lose precision if context is tight. I will flag it as uncertain/low risk, but the release bug is definite.

Logic error: cancel_order calls inventory.release(order) which adds stock back, but if the order was never successfully reserved (e.g. status is "placed" but reservation failed? No, place_order sets status to "placed" only after successful reserve. However, if cancel_order is called on an order that was "placed", it releases stock. But release has the bug mentioned above. Also, if cancel_order is called twice, it will release stock twice, inflating inventory. There is no guard against double cancellation.
Logic error: release assigns item.qty to stock instead of adding it (+=), corrupting inventory counts.
State consistency bug: reserve deducts stock incrementally; if a subsequent item fails availability, previous deductions are not rolled back, violating the "all or nothing" guarantee.

reported: Resource leak: the httpx.Client is created in __init__ but if close() is never called (or the object is not used as a context manager), the underlying connection pool is never released. The class should implement __del__ as a safety net to call close().

Off-by-one error: attempt starts at 0, so the exponential delay sequence on transient retries is 0.5(20)jitter = ~0.25s, 0.5(21)jitter = ~0.75s, etc. This skips the intended base_delay (0.5s) for the first retry. It should be 2  (attempt - 1) or use attempt + 1 to correctly yield ~0.5s on the first retry.

Incorrect Retry-After parsing: the HTTP Retry-After header can be either an HTTP-date or a delay-seconds integer. Passing it directly to float() will raise ValueError for date formats (caught by the try-except) but if it's a numeric string, min(float("60"), 30.0) incorrectly caps a requested 60s delay to 30s. The code then falls through to the exponential backoff, overriding the server's explicit retry directive and potentially causing a 429 loop.

Exception suppression: __exit__ returns True, which unconditionally swallows any exception raised within the with block, silently masking errors. It should return False (or implicitly None) to propagate exceptions properly.

Misleading/missing exception on transport exhaustion: if the loop ends after exhausting max_attempts on TransportErrors, last_exc is set and properly chained. However, if it exhausts attempts on retryable HTTP statuses (like 429/503), last_exc remains None, chaining a NoneType which is misleading. The RuntimeError should explicitly cover the unresponsive status code scenario.

reported: Mutable default aliasing: config = DEFAULTS assigns the reference of the module-level DEFAULTS dict to config. Any subsequent .update() or key assignment modifies the global DEFAULTS, causing state leakage between calls.

Logical error in boolean coercion: bool(value) returns True for any non-empty string (including "false", "0", "no"). It does not parse semantic boolean strings, leading to incorrect configuration values.

Resource leak / Data loss risk: If os.replace(tmp, path) fails (e.g., due to permissions or disk full), the temporary file remains on disk. More critically, if this function is interrupted between write and replace, or if os.replace raises an exception after partial writes in other contexts, it lacks cleanup. However, the primary bug here is that os.replace is atomic on POSIX but not necessarily on all Windows setups if the target exists and is open, but strictly speaking, the lack of try/finally to remove tmp on exception is a resource leak.

Security/Robustness: json.load(f) without restricting object_hook or parse_float can be susceptible to denial-of-service via deeply nested JSON or float parsing issues, though less critical than the others. More importantly, if the JSON file contains keys not in DEFAULTS, they are added to config. Later, validate() (line 41) checks for unknown keys. If the JSON file has extra keys, validate will raise an error. This is a design flaw/bug because load_config updates config with JSON data before checking env vars, but validate rejects any key not in DEFAULTS. This means you cannot extend config via JSON file at all, which might be intended, but combined with line 26 bug, it's messy. However, the most direct "defect" is that validate is called after env vars override JSON. If JSON has valid keys and env vars have valid keys, it works. But if JSON has an unknown key, it crashes. This is likely intended behavior, so not a bug per se.

Type error risk: int(value) will raise a ValueError if the environment variable string is not a valid integer literal (e.g., "8080.0" or "eight"). There is no try/except block, causing the application to crash on invalid env var input instead of using the default or providing a useful error.
Assigning config = DEFAULTS creates a reference to the mutable module-level dictionary; subsequent .update() calls modify DEFAULTS directly, causing state leakage across function invocations.
bool(value) evaluates to True for any non-empty string (e.g., "false", "0"), failing to correctly parse semantic boolean environment variables.

claims.quote: previous studies estimate that 30–69% of LLM-generated references in biomedical contexts are fabricated.
claims.claim: Establishes a pre-existing published range of 30–69% fabrication for LLM-generated biomedical references, cited by The Lancet's own audit.

claims.quote: Among 97·1 million verified references, we identified 4046 fabricated references across 2810 papers
claims.claim: Of 2.5 million papers audited, 2,810 contained at least one fabricated reference — fabricated citations are present in the actual peer-reviewed literature, not just in raw LLM output.

claims.quote: In 2023, approximately one in 2828 papers contained at least one fabricated reference. By 2025, this had risen to one in 458 and in the first 7 weeks of 2026, one in 277 papers had at least one fabricated reference.
claims.claim: The rate of fabricated references appearing in published biomedical papers increased roughly tenfold from 2023 to early 2026.

claims.quote: Our results show that the observed hallucination rates span a fivefold range (between 11.4% and 56.8%) and are strongly shaped by model, domain, and prompt framing.
claims.claim: Across 10 commercial LLMs generating 69,557 citations, fabrication rates ranged from 11.4% to 56.8% depending on model, domain, and prompt.

claims.quote: no model spontaneously generates citations when unprompted, which seems to establish hallucination as prompt-induced rather than intrinsic.
claims.claim: Citation fabrication only occurs when the model is explicitly asked to provide citations — it is not something models do unprompted.

claims.quote: Across the 6 reviews, GPT-4o generated 176 citations; 35 (19.9%) were fabricated. Among the 141 real citations, 64 (45.4%) contained errors, most frequently incorrect or invalid digital object identifiers.
claims.claim: GPT-4o fabricated ~20% of citations overall, and nearly half of the real citations still had bibliographic errors.

claims.quote: Fabrication rates differed significantly by disorder (χ22=13.7; P=.001), with higher rates for binge eating disorder (17/60, 28%) and body dysmorphic disorder (14/48, 29%) than for major depressive disorder (4/68, 6%).
claims.claim: Fabrication rate varies substantially by topic — less publicly familiar or less-researched topics produce ~5x higher fabrication rates.

claims.quote: We benchmark 13 state-of-the-art LLMs on citation generation across 40 research domains, finding that all models hallucinate citations at rates from 14.23% to 94.93%, with significant variation across research domains.
claims.claim: Across 13 LLMs, citation fabrication rates ranged from ~14% to ~95%; every model fabricated some citations.

claims.quote: we analyze 2.2 million citations from 56,381 papers published at top-tier AI/ML and Security venues (2020–2025), confirming that 1.07% of papers contain invalid or fabricated citations (604 papers), with an 80.9% increase in 2025 alone.
claims.claim: Fabricated citations have already contaminated top-tier peer-reviewed venues, and the rate is accelerating.

claims.quote: 41.5% of researchers copy-paste BibTeX without checking and 44.4% choose no-action responses when encountering suspicious references; meanwhile, 76.7% of reviewers do not thoroughly check references and 80.0% never suspect fake citations.
claims.claim: Survey data (n=94) shows a systemic verification gap — most researchers and reviewers do not verify references, enabling fabricated citations to pass peer review.

claims.quote: Fabrication ranged from 10.2% (Claude Opus 4.8, which declined 52.1% of prompts) to 98.4% (Ministral 3B, which produced no verifiable reference).
claims.claim: Across 26 LLMs, fabrication rates varied enormously by model — from ~10% (with heavy refusal) to ~98%.

claims.quote: Across all models, 55.4% of responses were fabricated and 14.9% were correct in every field.
claims.claim: In aggregate across all 26 models tested on biomedical references, over half of generated citations were fabricated, and only ~15% were fully accurate.

claims.quote: Models that identify real papers may still misstate their metadata, so references produced with model assistance require verification before use.
claims.claim: Even when models find real papers, they frequently get bibliographic fields (authors, journal, year, DOI) wrong.

reported: Timing attack vulnerability: Using the != operator for MAC comparison allows an attacker to determine the correct HMAC byte-by-byte based on response time. It must use hmac.compare_digest(mac, expected) to perform a constant-time comparison.

Insecure password hashing: Using a single round of SHA-256 for password hashing is cryptographically weak and makes the hash vulnerable to brute-force and rainbow table attacks. A dedicated password hashing algorithm (like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) or at least hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac with a high iteration count must be used.

Resource leak (memory): Expired sessions are only deleted from self.sessions when get_user is called, but sessions that are never accessed again are never removed, causing self.sessions to grow indefinitely. There is no cleanup mechanism for abandoned sessions.

Stale sessions resource leak: destroy_all_for removes the session entries from self.sessions but does not invalidate the corresponding signed tokens. If an attacker possesses a valid signed token for a destroyed session, they can continue to use it indefinitely (since the session store is vulnerable to replays, see below) or the missing server-side state won't prevent the client from believing they are still authenticated.

Replay vulnerability: Session tokens lack a generation or version counter. If a user changes their password or their session is explicitly destroyed, previously issued tokens remain cryptographically valid and cannot be universally revoked without mapping tokens to users.

Replay vulnerability across sessions: Because destroy_all_for deletes server-side entries but the tokens remain valid signatures, an attacker who steals a token can replay it even after destroy_all_for is called, provided they can cause a new session to be created with the same session_id (re-registration or session ID collision). While session_id is random, the architecture's lack of token invalidation is a fundamental security flaw.

reported: reserve violates its documented "reserve every item of the order, or nothing at all" contract: stock is decremented inside the loop (line 39) before later items have been checked, so if item N fails the availability check, items 1..N-1 have already been decremented and that mutation is never rolled back. The function returns False but leaves partial reservations in self.stock. The correct pattern is to verify all items first in one pass, then decrement in a second pass (or snapshot/restore on failure).

release overwrites stock instead of restoring it: self.stock[item.sku] = item.qty sets the on-hand quantity to the order line's quantity, discarding whatever was already there. It must be self.stock[item.sku] += item.qty. Concretely, if stock started at 10, an order reserved 2 (stock → 8), then cancel_order calls release, stock becomes 2 instead of 10 — silent inventory corruption. This also breaks if two items in the same order share a SKU: each iteration clobbers the previous one's result.

The DEFAULTS dictionary is assigned directly to config rather than copied. This mutates the module-level global DEFAULTS object when config.update() or environment variables modify config, causing state to leak across calls.

with_suffix(".tmp") replaces the existing suffix of the path. For a path like "conf.json", it results in "conf.tmp", but for a path like "conf" (no suffix), it results in "conf.tmp" as intended. If the path has a trailing dot or unexpected suffix format, it could behave unexpectedly or collide with other files.

If the JSON file contains unknown keys, config.update(json.load(f)) adds them to config. The subsequent validate(config) call on line 36 then raises a ValueError, which crashes the function while the with p.open() block safely closes the file, but leaves the application unable to load a file with extra keys.

reported: The loop condition while d < end excludes end itself, contradicting the docstring "from start to end, inclusive" — e.g. daterange(date(2024,1,1), date(2024,1,31)) stops at Jan 30, and if start == end nothing is yielded at all. This off-by-one also silently makes business_days (line 14) undercount, since the end date is never considered; the condition should be while d <= end.

The quarter formula is wrong: d.month // 3 + 1 maps March to Q2, June to Q3, September to Q4, and December to "Q5" (an invalid value). The correct formula is (d.month - 1) // 3 + 1 (or (d.month + 2) // 3).

If the loop exits because of retryable HTTP status codes (no transport exception ever occurred), last_exc remains None, causing raise RuntimeError(...) from None which obscures the true cause of the failure (the last HTTP response/status code).

reported: Partial reservation bug: reserve() decrements stock as it iterates, so if a later item fails the availability check the earlier decrements are not rolled back — the "all or nothing" guarantee is broken and inventory is silently leaked.

release() assigns (self.stock[item.sku] = item.qty) instead of restoring (+=), so it overwrites the current stock level rather than adding back the reserved quantity, destroying any stock that was there (or reserved by other orders).

place_order() never validates that item quantities or prices are non-negative; reserve() will happily process qty <= 0, meaning a negative quantity increases stock on reservation (and decreases it again on release), and produces a negative subtotal. Combined with the line 44 bug this is exploitable to corrupt inventory.

The hit_rate method will raise a ZeroDivisionError if it is called before any get calls have been made (i.e., when total is 0). It should return 0.0 (or handle the division by zero) in that case.

claims.quote: A specific sequence of customer configuration changes, performed across two different control plane build versions, resulted in incompatible customer configuration metadata being generated. These customer configuration changes themselves were valid and non-malicious – however they produced metadata that, when deployed to edge site servers, exposed a latent bug in the data plane. This incompatibility triggered a crash during asynchronous processing within the data plane service.
claims.claim: Root cause was valid customer configs across control plane versions creating incompatible metadata that triggered a data plane crash bug, leading to global edge site failures and DNS issues.

claims.quote: The issue was not caused, directly or indirectly, by a cyber attack or malicious activity of any kind. Instead, it was triggered by a change to one of our database systems’ permissions which caused the database to output multiple entries into a “feature file” used by our Bot Management system. That feature file, in turn, doubled in size. The larger-than-expected feature file was then propagated to all the machines that make up our network.
claims.claim: Root cause was a database permissions change generating an oversized Bot Management feature file that propagated network-wide and crashed traffic routing software due to a size limit.

claims.quote: The issue was not caused, directly or indirectly, by a cyber attack on Cloudflare’s systems or malicious activity of any kind. Instead, it was triggered by changes being made to our body parsing logic while attempting to detect and mitigate an industry-wide vulnerability disclosed this week in React Server Components.
claims.claim: Root cause was body parsing logic changes for React vulnerability mitigation triggering a Lua error state in the FL1 proxy, causing HTTP 500 errors.

claims.quote: The incident’s impact stemmed from several issues, but the immediate trigger was a bug in the dashboard. This bug caused repeated, unnecessary calls to the Tenant Service API. The API calls were managed by a React useEffect hook, but we mistakenly included a problematic object in its dependency array. Because this object was recreated on every state or prop change, React treated it as “always new,” causing the useEffect to re-run each time.
claims.claim: Root cause was a React useEffect bug in the Dashboard causing excessive Tenant Service API calls, overwhelming the service.

claims.quote: The outage occurred because of a misconfiguration of legacy systems used to maintain the infrastructure that advertises Cloudflare’s IP addresses to the Internet.
claims.claim: Root cause was a legacy system misconfiguration that incorrectly advertised 1.1.1.1 prefixes, dormant until a service topology change activated it.
